Supervised learning asks a question with a known answer. Clustering asks the data what groups it contains, and the data always answers — even when there are no groups. You will meet the five families of clustering algorithm the laboratory uses (centroid, hierarchical, density-based, model-based and the chemistry-specific leader algorithms), the distance functions that make them meaningful on each of our data types, and the validity machinery that decides whether a partition deserves to be in a paper. Four lab tasks run through the unit: detect the chemical series inside the ROCK1 dataset, pick a diverse subset and prove it is more diverse than a random one, extract metastable conformations from a replica molecular-dynamics ensemble, and ask whether the gingival expression slice contains patient subgroups. It ends with the error unsupervised learning invites most often: reading clusters off a t-SNE picture of data that has none.

Resumen en español

Esta unidad trata el aprendizaje no supervisado. Se estudian k-medias (con su geometría, su costo y sus modos de falla), el agrupamiento jerárquico aglomerativo con sus distintos enlaces y el dendrograma, los métodos basados en densidad (DBSCAN, OPTICS, HDBSCAN), las mezclas de gaussianas seleccionadas por BIC y el algoritmo de Butina sobre huellas moleculares. Se eligen métricas de distancia acordes al tipo de dato: euclidiana sobre descriptores estandarizados, Tanimoto sobre huellas binarias, RMSD sobre conformaciones y correlación sobre perfiles de expresión. Se validan las particiones con índices internos (silueta, Davies-Bouldin), externos (índice de Rand ajustado) y con estabilidad bajo remuestreo, mostrando los límites del método del codo. Finalmente se resuelven cuatro tareas del laboratorio - detección de series químicas, selección de un subconjunto diverso, conformaciones metaestables de dinámica molecular y subgrupos de pacientes - y se advierte sobre los grupos que no existen en los mapas t-SNE.

Learning objectives

  • Apply k-means, hierarchical (agglomerative), DBSCAN/HDBSCAN, Gaussian mixtures and Butina/leader clustering, and choose among them from the data's geometry and from the question being asked.
  • Choose distance metrics appropriate to the data type: Euclidean on standardised descriptors, Tanimoto/Jaccard on fingerprints, RMSD on conformations, correlation on expression profiles.
  • Validate a clustering with internal indices (silhouette, Davies-Bouldin, Calinski-Harabasz), external indices (adjusted Rand index) and stability under resampling, and resist over-interpretation.
  • Use clustering for the laboratory's practical tasks: diversity selection, series identification, representative conformations and patient subgroups.
  • Explain why an elbow appears in data that has no clusters, and why clusters appear in a t-SNE map of pure noise.

1. What clustering is, and what it is not

A clustering algorithm takes $n$ objects and returns a label for each one without ever seeing a target variable. Everything that makes supervised learning self-correcting — a held-out score, a learning curve, a y-scrambling control — has to be rebuilt by hand here, and most published clusterings do not bother; Jain's survey of fifty years of the field opens with exactly that complaint[1].

Three distinctions organise the whole unit.

  1. The question comes before the algorithm. "Which compounds belong to the same series?" is answered with Tanimoto distances and a leader algorithm; "which 50 compounds should we buy?" is a coverage question answered by a diversity picker, not by a clustering at all.
  2. The metric is a modelling decision, not a detail. Two molecules are "close" in descriptor space, in fingerprint space and in scaffold space in three different and only weakly related senses, as Section 8 measures explicitly.
  3. A partition is a hypothesis. It must be checked internally (are the clusters compact and separated?), externally (do they agree with something known?) and for stability (does a different sample give the same partition?).

Domain context — what a "cluster" means in each of our data sets

Compounds. Medicinal chemists work in series: one core structure (a scaffold, formally the Bemis-Murcko framework — the molecule stripped of side chains[23]) decorated with dozens of substituent variations, so a cluster of compounds should ideally recover a series. A Morgan fingerprint[22] encodes a molecule as a bit vector, each bit recording one circular atom environment up to radius 2 hashed into 2,048 positions.

Conformations. A molecular-dynamics (MD) simulation integrates Newton's equations for a protein in water and writes a frame of coordinates every few picoseconds. Our frozen ensemble is the 20-residue Trp-cage miniprotein (PDB 1L2Y), six independent 1 ns runs: three at 300 K (condition A), three at 340 K (condition B). The frames are superposed on a common reference, so the Euclidean distance between two C-alpha coordinate vectors divided by $\sqrt{N}$ is their root-mean-square deviation (RMSD) in nanometres. A cluster of frames is a candidate metastable conformation.

Patients. The expression slice holds log2 microarray intensities for 5,000 genes in 138 gingival-tissue biopsies from 69 patients, one diseased and one healthy site each[31]. A cluster of samples is a candidate molecular subtype, a claim made for this very cohort[30].

2. Distance first: four metrics for four kinds of data

Every clustering algorithm in this unit is a rule for grouping objects that are close. Fix the notion of closeness and you have already decided most of the result.

Euclidean distance on standardised features. $d(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}) = \sqrt{\sum_j (x_j-y_j)^2}$. The sum is over columns, so molecular weight in daltons (hundreds) would swamp logP in log units (single digits): standardising each column to mean 0 and standard deviation 1 is what makes the sum meaningful. Even then, correlated columns count twice.

Tanimoto (Jaccard) distance on binary fingerprints. For bit vectors $a,b$, $$ S_{\text{Tanimoto}}(a,b)=\frac{|a \cap b|}{|a|+|b|-|a \cap b|}, \qquad d = 1 - S .$$ The numerator counts bits set in both molecules, the denominator counts bits set in either. Zeros shared by two molecules — both lack a nitro group, both lack a sugar — contribute nothing, which is the whole point: in a 2,048-bit fingerprint with about fifty bits set, shared absence is uninformative and Euclidean distance would be dominated by it[24].

RMSD on conformations. After optimal superposition, $\text{RMSD}=\sqrt{\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\|\mathbf{r}_i-\mathbf{r}'_i\|^2}$ over $N$ selected atoms. It is a Euclidean distance in $3N$ dimensions divided by $\sqrt{N}$, which is why we can hand superposed coordinates straight to a Euclidean algorithm and read the answer in nanometres[25].

Correlation distance on expression profiles. $d = 1-r$ with $r$ the Pearson correlation between two profiles: two patients whose genes move together are close even if one array is globally brighter. Correlation distance discards the level and keeps the shape — usually right for microarray samples, never right for molecular weight.

2.1 A worked example by hand

Take two small aromatic fragments: pyridine (c1ccncc1) and benzene (c1ccccc1). With a Morgan radius-1 fingerprint folded into 64 bits, suppose pyridine sets bits $\{a,b,c,d\}$ and benzene the subset $\{a,b\}$. Then $|a\cap b| = 2$, $|a|=4$, $|b|=2$, so

$$S = \frac{2}{4+2-2} = 0.5, \qquad d_{\text{Tanimoto}} = 0.5 .$$

The next cell computes the real fingerprints and checks the arithmetic, then does the same for the first two compounds of the ROCK1 table.

# Worked example 1: Tanimoto by hand vs RDKit.
g64 = rdFingerprintGenerator.GetMorganGenerator(radius=1, fpSize=64)
pyr, ben = Chem.MolFromSmiles("c1ccncc1"), Chem.MolFromSmiles("c1ccccc1")
fa, fb = g64.GetFingerprint(pyr), g64.GetFingerprint(ben)
A, B = set(fa.GetOnBits()), set(fb.GetOnBits())
inter, union = len(A & B), len(A | B)
print(f"pyridine bits {sorted(A)}  benzene bits {sorted(B)}")
print(f"|A|={len(A)}  |B|={len(B)}  |A and B|={inter}  |A or B|={union}")
print(f"by hand  S = {inter}/{union} = {inter/union:.4f}   d = {1-inter/union:.4f}")
print(f"RDKit    S = {DataStructs.TanimotoSimilarity(fa, fb):.4f}   "
      f"d = {1-DataStructs.TanimotoSimilarity(fa, fb):.4f}")

# The same two quantities on the 2048-bit fingerprints of the first two ROCK1 compounds.
s01 = DataStructs.TanimotoSimilarity(fps[0], fps[1])
eucl01 = float(np.linalg.norm(Xfp[0] - Xfp[1]))
print(f"\nROCK1 compounds 0 and 1: Tanimoto similarity {s01:.3f} (distance {1-s01:.3f}); "
      f"Euclidean distance between the same bit vectors {eucl01:.2f}")
print(f"bits set: {int(Xfp[0].sum())} and {int(Xfp[1].sum())} of 2048 "
      f"-> {2048 - int(((Xfp[0]+Xfp[1])>0).sum())} bits are zero in both and are ignored by Tanimoto")

pyridine bits [0, 3, 10, 17, 58]  benzene bits [0, 17]
|A|=5  |B|=2  |A and B|=2  |A or B|=5
by hand  S = 2/5 = 0.4000   d = 0.6000
RDKit    S = 0.4000   d = 0.6000

ROCK1 compounds 0 and 1: Tanimoto similarity 0.160 (distance 0.840); Euclidean distance between the same bit vectors 8.25
bits set: 51 and 43 of 2048 -> 1967 bits are zero in both and are ignored by Tanimoto

The hand calculation and RDKit agree exactly, which is the only way to be sure you know what a similarity function counts. Of 2,048 bits the overwhelming majority are zero in both molecules: a Euclidean distance between the same vectors has no chemical scale, whereas Tanimoto distance is bounded in $[0,1]$ and has a conventional reading — below about 0.35 (similarity above 0.65) two Morgan fingerprints usually belong to the same series[21].

2.2 The cost of a distance matrix

Most algorithms below need all $n(n-1)/2$ pairwise distances: 3.8 million numbers for our 2,764 compounds (trivial), $5\times10^9$ for a 100,000-compound catalogue (about 20 GB, impossible on a laptop). Production pipelines therefore use sparse neighbour lists or algorithms that never materialise the matrix. Plan the memory before launching.

# Distance-matrix cost, measured rather than asserted.
rows = []
for n in [500, 1000, 2000, len(fps)]:
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    d = pdist(Xfp[:n], metric="jaccard").astype(np.float32)
    rows.append({"n": n, "pairs": n*(n-1)//2, "MB (float32)": n*(n-1)/2*4/1e6,
                 "seconds": time.perf_counter() - t0})
cost = pd.DataFrame(rows)
cost["MB (float32)"] = cost["MB (float32)"].round(1); cost["seconds"] = cost["seconds"].round(3)
print(cost.to_string(index=False))
print(f"\nextrapolated to a 100,000-compound library: "
      f"{100000*99999/2/1e9:.1f} billion pairs = {100000*99999/2*4/1e9:.0f} GB in float32")

   n   pairs  MB (float32)  seconds
 500  124750           0.5    0.236
1000  499500           2.0    0.921
2000 1999000           8.0    3.680
2764 3818466          15.3    6.960

extrapolated to a 100,000-compound library: 5.0 billion pairs = 20 GB in float32

The measured times confirm the quadratic law: quadrupling $n$ multiplies the work by about sixteen, and the extrapolation to a vendor catalogue is the practical message — the algorithm must be chosen to avoid building that matrix at all.

3. k-means: the centroid family

k-means minimises the within-cluster sum of squares (inertia)

$$ J=\sum_{k=1}^{K}\sum_{i \in C_k} \| \mathbf{x}_i - \boldsymbol{\mu}_k \|^2 , \qquad \boldsymbol{\mu}_k=\frac{1}{|C_k|}\sum_{i \in C_k}\mathbf{x}_i . $$

Lloyd's algorithm[2] alternates two steps that each can only decrease $J$: assign every point to its nearest centroid, then update every centroid to the mean of its members. It converges to a local minimum that depends on the initial centroids, which is why scikit-learn restarts it n_init times from k-means++ seeds[3]. Cost per iteration is $O(nKd)$ with no distance matrix, so k-means scales to millions of rows.

Assumptions. Minimising squared Euclidean distances to a mean implies clusters that are spherical, of similar spread and of similar size, and a mean that is a meaningful object: the mean of a set of fingerprints is not a molecule. Section 8 applies k-means to fingerprints deliberately, to show what it costs.

3.1 A worked example by hand

Six points on a line: $x = 1, 2, 3, 10, 11, 12$, with $K=2$ and the unlucky initial centroids $\mu_1 = 2$, $\mu_2 = 11$ replaced by a deliberately bad pair, $\mu_1 = 1$ and $\mu_2 = 2$.

step $\mu_1$ $\mu_2$ assignment $J$
start 1.00 2.00 $\{1\}$, $\{2,3,10,11,12\}$ $0 + (2-7.6)^2+(3-7.6)^2+(10-7.6)^2+(11-7.6)^2+(12-7.6)^2 = 85.2$
after update 1 1.00 7.60 $\{1,2,3\}$, $\{10,11,12\}$ $2 + 2 = 4.0$
after update 2 2.00 11.00 $\{1,2,3\}$, $\{10,11,12\}$ $2 + 2 = 4.0$ — converged

Two iterations suffice even from a bad start; the cell below reproduces the trace.

# Worked example 2: Lloyd's algorithm by hand on six points, then scikit-learn.
x = np.array([1., 2., 3., 10., 11., 12.]).reshape(-1, 1)
mu = np.array([1.0, 2.0])
for step in range(4):
    lab = np.argmin(np.abs(x - mu), axis=1)
    J = float(sum(((x[lab == k] - mu[k])**2).sum() for k in range(2)))
    print(f"step {step}: centroids {np.round(mu,2)}  assignment {lab}  J = {J:.1f}")
    new = np.array([x[lab == k].mean() if (lab == k).any() else mu[k] for k in range(2)])
    if np.allclose(new, mu):
        print("converged"); break
    mu = new

from sklearn.cluster import KMeans
km6 = KMeans(n_clusters=2, n_init=10, random_state=0).fit(x)
print(f"\nscikit-learn: centroids {np.sort(km6.cluster_centers_.ravel()).round(2)}  "
      f"inertia {km6.inertia_:.1f}  labels {km6.labels_}")

step 0: centroids [1. 2.]  assignment [0 1 1 1 1 1]  J = 246.0
step 1: centroids [1.  7.6]  assignment [0 0 0 1 1 1]  J = 41.7
step 2: centroids [ 2. 11.]  assignment [0 0 0 1 1 1]  J = 4.0
converged

scikit-learn: centroids [ 2. 11.]  inertia 4.0  labels [1 1 1 0 0 0]

The hand trace and scikit-learn agree: centroids 2 and 11, inertia 4.0. The intermediate line is the lesson — the partition is already correct after the first update, while the inertia fell from 85.2 to 4.0. A bad initialisation shows up as a stalled $J$, not as an error message.

3.2 k-means on the compound descriptors

Now the real table: 2,764 compounds in 11 standardised descriptor dimensions, with $K$ swept from 2 to 10 and four quantities recorded at each $K$ — inertia, mean silhouette (Section 7), Davies-Bouldin, Calinski-Harabasz — plus the size of the smallest cluster, the diagnostic most people forget.

# k-means sweep over K on the standardised descriptors.
from sklearn.metrics import silhouette_score, davies_bouldin_score, calinski_harabasz_score
sweep = []
for K in range(2, 11):
    km = KMeans(n_clusters=K, n_init=10, random_state=0).fit(Zdesc)
    sizes = np.bincount(km.labels_)
    sweep.append({"K": K, "inertia": km.inertia_,
                  "silhouette": silhouette_score(Zdesc, km.labels_),
                  "davies_bouldin": davies_bouldin_score(Zdesc, km.labels_),
                  "calinski_harabasz": calinski_harabasz_score(Zdesc, km.labels_),
                  "smallest cluster": int(sizes.min())})
sweep = pd.DataFrame(sweep)
print(sweep.round(3).to_string(index=False))
best_sil = int(sweep.loc[sweep["silhouette"].idxmax(), "K"])
best_db = int(sweep.loc[sweep["davies_bouldin"].idxmin(), "K"])
print(f"\nsilhouette prefers K = {best_sil}; Davies-Bouldin prefers K = {best_db}; "
      f"inertia prefers the largest K on offer, as it always does")

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(9.4, 2.9))
axes[0].plot(sweep["K"], sweep["inertia"], "o-", color="#36c")
axes[0].set_xlabel("K"); axes[0].set_ylabel("inertia (within-cluster SS)"); axes[0].set_title("Inertia: monotone")

silhouette range over the sweep: 0.189 to 0.291

Figure 1. k-means on 2,764 compounds in 11 standardised descriptor dimensions. Inertia (left) falls monotonically and therefore cannot select K; the mean silhouette (centre) peaks at the smallest K on offer, where Davies-Bouldin (right) also has its minimum. The whole silhouette range sits well below 0.3: descriptor space is a continuum, not a set of separated groups.

The silhouette never rises above about 0.3: the average compound is almost as close to its neighbouring cluster as to its own, so the partition is a convenient subdivision of a cloud, not a discovery of structure. Reporting "we identified K chemical classes by k-means" from such a sweep is the commonest unsupervised-learning error in the medicinal-chemistry literature.

3.3 Three geometries where k-means fails

The assumptions are easy to state and easy to violate. The next cell builds three synthetic data sets of 600 points each where the ground truth is known, and compares k-means with the ground truth by the adjusted Rand index (ARI, Section 7): 1.0 is a perfect match, 0.0 is chance.

# Three synthetic geometries: anisotropic, unequal variance, unequal size.
from sklearn.datasets import make_blobs, make_moons
from sklearn.metrics import adjusted_rand_score as ari
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
Xa, ya = make_blobs(n_samples=600, centers=3, cluster_std=0.8, random_state=0)
Xa = Xa @ np.array([[0.60, -0.64], [-0.40, 0.85]])                      # anisotropic (sheared)
Xv, yv = make_blobs(n_samples=600, cluster_std=[1.0, 3.0, 0.4], random_state=0)   # unequal variance
Xs0, ys0 = make_blobs(n_samples=1500, centers=3, cluster_std=0.9, random_state=0)
keep = np.hstack([np.where(ys0 == 0)[0][:500], np.where(ys0 == 1)[0][:50], np.where(ys0 == 2)[0][:50]])
Xs, ys = Xs0[keep], ys0[keep]                                           # unequal size 500/50/50
Xm, ym = make_moons(n_samples=600, noise=0.06, random_state=0)           # non-convex

cases = [("anisotropic", Xa, ya), ("unequal variance", Xv, yv),
         ("unequal size 500/50/50", Xs, ys), ("two moons", Xm, ym)]
for name, Xc, yc in cases:
    lab = KMeans(n_clusters=len(np.unique(yc)), n_init=10, random_state=0).fit_predict(Xc)
    print(f"{name:24s} K={len(np.unique(yc))}  ARI(k-means, truth) = {ari(yc, lab):.3f}  "
          f"cluster sizes {np.sort(np.bincount(lab))[::-1]}")

# Figure 2: what those failures look like.
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 4, figsize=(9.4, 4.6))
for j, (name, Xc, yc) in enumerate(cases):
    lab = KMeans(n_clusters=len(np.unique(yc)), n_init=10, random_state=0).fit_predict(Xc)
    axes[0, j].scatter(Xc[:, 0], Xc[:, 1], c=yc, s=5, cmap="viridis")
    axes[0, j].set_title(f"{name}\ntruth", fontsize=8.5)
    axes[1, j].scatter(Xc[:, 0], Xc[:, 1], c=lab, s=5, cmap="viridis")
    axes[1, j].set_title(f"k-means, ARI = {ari(yc, lab):.2f}", fontsize=8.5)
    for a in (axes[0, j], axes[1, j]):
        a.set_xticks([]); a.set_yticks([])
fig.tight_layout()

unequal variance         K=3  ARI(k-means, truth) = 0.487  cluster sizes [274 227  99]

Figure 2. Top row, ground truth; bottom row, k-means with the correct K. Sheared clusters are cut across their long axis; a wide cluster beside a narrow one is dismembered; a 500/50/50 split is rebalanced towards equal sizes; two interleaved crescents defeat any straight-boundary partition. The adjusted Rand indices above quantify each failure.

Each failure has a fix: shear and unequal variance are handled by a Gaussian mixture with full covariances (Section 6), unequal sizes by a density method that does not try to balance, non-convex shapes only by density or spectral methods. No amount of tuning K repairs any of them.

4. Hierarchical clustering: the whole family of partitions at once

Agglomerative clustering starts with $n$ singletons and repeatedly merges the two closest, producing a binary tree (dendrogram) whose every horizontal cut is a partition: you choose $K$ afterwards, a real advantage when $K$ is the question. "Closest" needs a definition for sets, and that is the linkage:

linkage distance between clusters $A,B$ behaviour
single $\min_{a\in A,b\in B} d(a,b)$ follows filaments; chains clusters together through bridges of points
complete $\max_{a\in A,b\in B} d(a,b)$ compact, equal-diameter clusters; sensitive to outliers
average (UPGMA) mean of all pairs compromise; the chemoinformatics default
Ward increase in within-cluster sum of squares caused by the merge[8] spherical, similar-sized clusters; only valid with Euclidean distances[9]

Cost is $O(n^2)$ memory, so a few tens of thousands of objects is the ceiling. The cophenetic correlation correlates each pair's original distance with the height at which the pair is first merged: near 1 the dendrogram is a faithful summary, low values mean the tree is an artefact of the linkage rule.

# Four linkages on a 600-compound descriptor subsample (n^2 memory), with cophenetic correlation.
sub = np.sort(np.random.default_rng(0).choice(len(Zdesc), 600, replace=False))
Dsub = pdist(Zdesc[sub])                       # Euclidean on standardised descriptors
trees, rows = {}, []
for meth in ["single", "complete", "average", "ward"]:
    Lk = linkage(Dsub, method=meth)
    trees[meth] = Lk
    coph = cophenet(Lk, Dsub)[0]
    lab4 = fcluster(Lk, 4, criterion="maxclust")
    rows.append({"linkage": meth, "cophenetic r": coph,
                 "K=4 sizes": np.sort(np.bincount(lab4)[1:])[::-1].tolist(),
                 "singletons at K=4": int((np.bincount(lab4)[1:] == 1).sum())})
print(pd.DataFrame(rows).to_string(index=False))

 linkage  cophenetic r          K=4 sizes  singletons at K=4
  single      0.595018     [597, 1, 1, 1]                  3
complete      0.498756   [412, 186, 1, 1]                  2
 average      0.707191    [577, 21, 1, 1]                  2
    ward      0.461836 [262, 178, 94, 66]                  0

# Figure 3: the same 600 compounds, four linkages, four dendrograms.
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 4, figsize=(9.4, 3.0))
for ax, meth in zip(axes, ["single", "complete", "average", "ward"]):
    dendrogram(trees[meth], no_labels=True, color_threshold=0, above_threshold_color="#444", ax=ax)
    ax.set_title(f"{meth}\ncophenetic r = {cophenet(trees[meth], Dsub)[0]:.2f}", fontsize=8.5)
    ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_ylabel("merge height" if meth == "single" else "")
fig.tight_layout()

Figure 3. Dendrograms of the same 600 compounds under four linkages. Single linkage (left) shows the staircase of chaining — almost every merge adds one more point to one growing cluster, so a cut at K = 4 gives one giant cluster plus singletons. Complete and average linkage give balanced trees, Ward the most balanced of all. The cophenetic correlations differ by linkage on identical data.

The table makes the chaining concrete: at $K=4$ single linkage returns singletons beside one giant cluster, while Ward returns four groups of comparable size. Neither is "right" — single linkage suits filaments (a congeneric series extended one substituent at a time really is a chain), Ward suits clusters you intend to summarise by a centroid. Choosing the linkage after seeing which gives the prettiest picture is a researcher degree of freedom: decide before you look, and say so in the methods.

5. Density-based clustering: DBSCAN, OPTICS and HDBSCAN

Density methods define a cluster as a connected region of high density and label the rest noise. DBSCAN[10] has two parameters, a radius $\varepsilon$ and a count min_samples: a point is a core point if at least min_samples points lie within $\varepsilon$, core points within $\varepsilon$ of each other join, non-core points within $\varepsilon$ of a core point are border points, everything else is noise.

Three properties follow. The number of clusters is an output, not a parameter; clusters may have any shape, because connectivity replaces convexity; and a point may be assigned to no cluster at all — what you want for screening data full of singleton chemotypes, and what breaks downstream code assuming every row has a label.

The weakness is structural: a single global $\varepsilon$ cannot serve regions of different density. The standard heuristic is the k-distance plot — sort every point's distance to its $k$-th nearest neighbour and look for a knee[10]. OPTICS[11] avoids committing to one $\varepsilon$ by ordering points so that the reachability profile shows clusters as valleys; HDBSCAN[12][13] builds a hierarchy over all density levels and keeps the clusters that persist longest. It ships with scikit-learn 1.3 and later as sklearn.cluster.HDBSCAN.

# k-distance plot and an eps sweep for DBSCAN on the descriptor space.
from sklearn.cluster import DBSCAN, OPTICS, HDBSCAN
from sklearn.neighbors import NearestNeighbors
MINPTS = 2 * Zdesc.shape[1]                     # the usual rule of thumb: 2 x dimensionality
nn = NearestNeighbors(n_neighbors=MINPTS).fit(Zdesc)
kdist = np.sort(nn.kneighbors(Zdesc)[0][:, -1])
knee = float(np.percentile(kdist, 95))
print(f"min_samples = {MINPTS}; {MINPTS}-th neighbour distance: median {np.median(kdist):.2f}, "
      f"95th percentile {knee:.2f}, max {kdist.max():.2f}")
dbrows = []
for eps in [0.8, 1.0, 1.2, 1.5, 2.0, 2.5]:
    lab = DBSCAN(eps=eps, min_samples=MINPTS).fit_predict(Zdesc)
    k = lab.max() + 1
    dbrows.append({"eps": eps, "clusters": k, "noise %": 100*(lab == -1).mean(),
                   "largest cluster %": 100*max([(lab == c).mean() for c in range(k)]) if k else 0.0})
print(pd.DataFrame(dbrows).round(2).to_string(index=False))

min_samples = 22; 22-th neighbour distance: median 1.38, 95th percentile 2.51, max 17.00

opt = OPTICS(min_samples=MINPTS, xi=0.05, min_cluster_size=0.02).fit(Zdesc)
reach = opt.reachability_[opt.ordering_]
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(9.4, 2.9))

axes[0].set_title("k-distance plot: knee near the 95th pct")

ax1b = axes[1].twinx()

axes[2].set_xlabel("OPTICS ordering"); axes[2].set_ylabel("reachability distance")
axes[2].set_title("OPTICS: valleys are clusters")
for a in axes: a.grid(alpha=.2)
fig.tight_layout()
print(f"OPTICS clusters: {opt.labels_.max()+1}, noise {100*(opt.labels_==-1).mean():.1f}%")

OPTICS clusters: 1, noise 97.9%

Figure 4. Left: the k-distance curve rises smoothly with no sharp knee — this cloud has no characteristic density scale. Centre: as eps grows, cluster count and noise fraction trade off, with everything noise at small eps and one cluster at large eps. Right: the OPTICS reachability profile is similarly featureless.

That negative result is worth more than a forced positive one: with no knee, no plateau and no valleys, the correct sentence is "no density-separated groups were found in descriptor space", not "DBSCAN identified four clusters (eps = 1.2)". To see the same algorithms succeed, apply them to the two-moons geometry where k-means failed and to a set with two densities.

# Density methods where they shine: non-convex shapes and unequal densities.
Xd = np.vstack([rng.normal(0, 0.25, (300, 2)), rng.normal([4, 4], 1.2, (300, 2)),
                rng.uniform(-6, 10, (120, 2))])              # dense blob, loose blob, uniform noise
yd = np.r_[np.zeros(300), np.ones(300), -np.ones(120)]
res = {}
for name, Xc, yc in [("two moons", Xm, ym), ("two densities + noise", Xd, yd)]:
    for alg, lab in [("k-means", KMeans(2, n_init=10, random_state=0).fit_predict(Xc)),
                     ("DBSCAN", DBSCAN(eps=0.3 if name == "two moons" else 0.6,
                                       min_samples=5).fit_predict(Xc)),
                     ("HDBSCAN", HDBSCAN(min_cluster_size=20, copy=True).fit_predict(Xc))]:
        res[(name, alg)] = lab
        print(f"{name:22s} {alg:8s} clusters {lab.max()+1:2d}  noise {100*(lab==-1).mean():5.1f}%  "
              f"ARI vs truth {ari(yc, lab):.3f}")

# Figure 5: three algorithms on two geometries.
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 3, figsize=(9.0, 5.0))
for i, (name, Xc) in enumerate([("two moons", Xm), ("two densities + noise", Xd)]):
    for j, alg in enumerate(["k-means", "DBSCAN", "HDBSCAN"]):
        lab = res[(name, alg)]

6. Model-based clustering: Gaussian mixtures and BIC

A Gaussian mixture model (GMM) assumes the data were generated by $K$ multivariate normals,

$$ p(\mathbf{x}) = \sum_{k=1}^{K} \pi_k \, \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{x} \mid \boldsymbol{\mu}_k, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_k), \qquad \sum_k \pi_k = 1,$$

and fits them by expectation-maximisation[14]: the E-step computes each point's responsibility $\gamma_{ik}$ (the posterior probability that component $k$ generated point $i$), the M-step re-estimates the parameters as responsibility-weighted statistics. k-means is the limit $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_k = \sigma^2 I$, $\sigma \to 0$, which is why a full-covariance GMM handles the sheared and unequal-variance geometries that defeated it. Being a probability model, a GMM has a likelihood and hence a principled way to compare $K$ and covariance structures: the Bayesian information criterion[16]

$$\mathrm{BIC} = -2\ln \hat{L} + p \ln n,$$

where $p$ is the number of free parameters and the $p\ln n$ term stops $K$ from growing without limit. Model-based clustering with BIC selection[15] is the closest thing clustering has to supervised model selection — with the caveat that it answers "how many Gaussians describe this density best", which is the same question as "how many groups are there" only if the groups are Gaussian.

# GMM: BIC over K and covariance type on the descriptor space.
from sklearn.mixture import GaussianMixture
bic = {}
for cov in ["spherical", "diag", "tied", "full"]:
    for K in range(1, 9):
        gm = GaussianMixture(K, covariance_type=cov, random_state=0, n_init=2).fit(Zdesc)
        bic[(cov, K)] = gm.bic(Zdesc)
tab = pd.DataFrame([{ "covariance": c, **{f"K={k}": bic[(c, k)] for k in range(1, 9)}}
                    for c in ["spherical", "diag", "tied", "full"]]).set_index("covariance")
print((tab/1000).round(1).to_string())    # thousands, for readability
best = min(bic, key=bic.get)
print(f"\nlowest BIC: covariance '{best[0]}' with K = {best[1]}  (BIC = {bic[best]:,.0f})")
gm_best = GaussianMixture(best[1], covariance_type=best[0], random_state=0, n_init=5).fit(Zdesc)
resp = gm_best.predict_proba(Zdesc)
print(f"mean maximum responsibility = {resp.max(1).mean():.3f}; "
      f"fraction of compounds with max responsibility < 0.8 = {(resp.max(1) < 0.8).mean():.1%}")

covariance

diag        86.5  75.9  72.2  70.2  53.0  42.4  39.0  38.5
tied        52.1  51.4  50.1  49.0  48.3  48.4  47.8  46.9

    axes[0].plot(range(1, 9), [bic[(cov, k)]/1000 for k in range(1, 9)], mk + "-", ms=4, label=cov)

Figure 6. Left: BIC against K for four covariance structures; richer covariances buy a much better likelihood and the winning curve keeps falling to the largest K examined — the mixture is modelling the shape of one continuous cloud. Right: each compound's maximum responsibility, with the 0.8 line marking the compounds the model cannot assign confidently.

The two diagnostics together tell the same story as Section 3: a flexible density model fits better and better as you give it more components, while the responsibilities show that a large share of compounds sit between components. A BIC that keeps falling is not evidence of many clusters; it is evidence that the density is not a mixture of a few well-separated Gaussians. The useful by-product is the soft assignment itself: unlike k-means, a GMM tells you which compounds are ambiguous, and those are exactly the ones you should not describe as members of a series.

Fit a full-covariance GMM with K = 3 to the anisotropic synthetic data of Section 3.3 and compute the ARI against the truth. 7. Validity: is this partition real?

Four questions, four tools.

Internal — compact and separated? The silhouette of point $i$[4] is

$$ s(i) = \frac{b(i)-a(i)}{\max\{a(i),b(i)\}} \in [-1,1], $$

with $a(i)$ the mean distance from $i$ to its own cluster and $b(i)$ to the nearest other cluster: $s \approx 1$ means comfortably inside, $s \approx 0$ on the boundary, $s<0$ in the wrong cluster. The Davies-Bouldin index[5] averages the worst ratio of within-cluster scatter to between-centroid distance (lower is better); the Calinski-Harabasz index[6] is a between/within variance ratio (higher is better). All three presuppose the kind of cluster k-means makes and penalise elongated DBSCAN clusters, so never use them to compare a density method with a centroid method.

The elbow, and why it is not evidence. The inertia curve always falls, so the eye is invited to find the $K$ where it stops falling fast. The trouble is that smooth, structureless data produces the same bend: squared error must drop quickly for the first few centroids in any cloud at all. The gap statistic[7] turns the heuristic into a comparison by measuring how much lower the observed $\log$ inertia is than the average $\log$ inertia of uniform reference data with the same bounding box,

$$ \mathrm{Gap}(K)=\mathbb{E}^{*}[\log W_K] - \log W_K ,$$

and choosing the smallest $K$ whose gap is within one standard error of the next. Run it on data that truly has no clusters and the gap stays flat at zero, which is the control every elbow plot is missing.

# The elbow on real data and on structureless data, plus a gap statistic for both.
U = rng.uniform(Zdesc.min(0), Zdesc.max(0), size=Zdesc.shape)     # same bounding box, no clusters
def inertia_curve(X, kmax=8):
    return np.array([KMeans(k, n_init=5, random_state=0).fit(X).inertia_ for k in range(1, kmax + 1)])
def gap_statistic(X, kmax=8, B=5, seed=0):
    r = np.random.default_rng(seed); lo, hi = X.min(0), X.max(0); out = []
    for k in range(1, kmax + 1):
        wk = np.log(KMeans(k, n_init=5, random_state=0).fit(X).inertia_)
        refs = [np.log(KMeans(k, n_init=5, random_state=0).fit(r.uniform(lo, hi, size=X.shape)).inertia_)
                for _ in range(B)]
        out.append((np.mean(refs) - wk, np.std(refs) * np.sqrt(1 + 1/B)))
    return np.array(out)
Ireal, Iunif = inertia_curve(Zdesc), inertia_curve(U)
Greal, Gunif = gap_statistic(Zdesc), gap_statistic(U, seed=1)
print("K  inertia/inertia(1) real  uniform     gap(real)   gap(uniform)+-SE")
for k in range(1, 9):
    print(f"{k}      {Ireal[k-1]/Ireal[0]:.3f}            {Iunif[k-1]/Iunif[0]:.3f}      "
          f"{Greal[k-1,0]:+.3f}      {Gunif[k-1,0]:+.3f} +- {Gunif[k-1,1]:.3f}")

K  inertia/inertia(1) real  uniform     gap(real)   gap(uniform)+-SE
1      1.000            1.000      +2.037      +0.013 +- 0.007
2      0.675            0.827      +2.233      +0.010 +- 0.007
3      0.593            0.740      +2.249      +0.004 +- 0.006
4      0.535            0.682      +2.263      -0.000 +- 0.005

7      0.423            0.619      +2.404      +0.001 +- 0.005
8      0.388            0.602      +2.461      -0.001 +- 0.002

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9.0, 3.0))
axes[0].plot(range(1, 9), Ireal/Ireal[0], "o-", color="#36c", label="ROCK1 descriptors")
axes[0].plot(range(1, 9), Iunif/Iunif[0], "s--", color="#c44", label="uniform noise, same box")

Figure 7. Left: inertia normalised by its K = 1 value for the real descriptors (blue) and for uniform noise in the same bounding box (red); both bend, so the shape of an elbow is not evidence of clusters. Right: the gap statistic sits at zero within its standard error at every K for the uniform reference — the correct answer — while for the real data it is large and keeps growing, singling out no K.

Read the two panels together: the elbow heuristic would have reported "three descriptor classes" for data generated by rng.uniform, while the gap statistic, which carries its own null model, refuses to. Every clustering claim needs at least one such control; where no gap statistic is defined, the resampling test below plays the same role.

7.1 Silhouette plots: look at the distribution, not the mean

A mean silhouette hides everything. The per-point silhouette plot shows how many points are actually negative — members assigned to a cluster they do not belong to.

# Silhouette distribution for K = 2 ... 5 on the descriptors.
from sklearn.metrics import silhouette_samples
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 4, figsize=(9.4, 3.1), sharex=True)
for ax, K in zip(axes, [2, 3, 4, 5]):
    lab = KMeans(K, n_init=10, random_state=0).fit_predict(Zdesc)
    sv = silhouette_samples(Zdesc, lab)
    low = 0
    for c in range(K):
        v = np.sort(sv[lab == c])
        ax.fill_betweenx(np.arange(low, low + len(v)), 0, v, color=plt.cm.viridis(c / max(K - 1, 1)))
        low += len(v) + 20
    ax.axvline(sv.mean(), color="#c44", ls="--", lw=1)
    ax.set_title(f"K = {K}\nmean {sv.mean():.3f}, {100*(sv<0).mean():.0f}% negative", fontsize=8.5)
    ax.set_yticks([]); ax.set_xlabel("silhouette")
fig.tight_layout()
for K in [2, 3, 4, 5]:
    lab = KMeans(K, n_init=10, random_state=0).fit_predict(Zdesc)
    sv = silhouette_samples(Zdesc, lab)
    print(f"K={K}: mean {sv.mean():.3f}, median {np.median(sv):.3f}, "
          f"negative {100*(sv<0).mean():.1f}%, worst cluster mean "
          f"{min(sv[lab==c].mean() for c in range(K)):.3f}")

K=3: mean 0.208, median 0.225, negative 7.2%, worst cluster mean 0.169

Figure 8. Per-compound silhouettes, sorted within each cluster, for K = 2 to 5; the dashed line is the mean. A healthy clustering shows wide knives of comparable length to the right of zero; here a substantial share is negative at every K and at least one cluster has a mean near zero.

7.2 External validity: the adjusted Rand index

When labels exist — the true generating classes in a simulation, the diseased/healthy status of a biopsy, the scaffold of a molecule — a partition can be compared with them. The Rand index is the fraction of object pairs that the two partitions treat consistently (together in both, or apart in both). Its flaw is that two random partitions already agree on many pairs, so Hubert and Arabie[17] subtracted the expectation:

$$ \mathrm{ARI} = \frac{\mathrm{RI}-\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{RI}]}{\max(\mathrm{RI})-\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{RI}]} ,$$

which is 0 for chance agreement, 1 for identity and can be slightly negative. The information-theoretic alternative, adjusted mutual information[18], behaves similarly and is preferable when clusters are very unbalanced. The next cell verifies the chance baseline by hand, which is the only way to trust it.

# ARI sanity checks: identical, permuted, random and split-in-two partitions.
from sklearn.metrics import adjusted_mutual_info_score as ami
lab3 = KMeans(3, n_init=10, random_state=0).fit_predict(Zdesc)
perm = np.array([2, 0, 1])[lab3]                              # relabelled, same partition
rand_lab = rng.integers(0, 3, len(lab3))                      # random labels
split = (lab3 == 0).astype(int)                               # coarser partition
print(f"ARI(lab, itself)            = {ari(lab3, lab3):.3f}")
print(f"ARI(lab, relabelled lab)    = {ari(lab3, perm):.3f}   <- invariant to label names")
print(f"ARI(lab, random labels)     = {ari(lab3, rand_lab):+.4f}  AMI = {ami(lab3, rand_lab):+.4f}  <- chance")
print(f"ARI(lab, coarser 2-cluster) = {ari(lab3, split):.3f}")
print(f"ARI over 200 random label vectors: mean {np.mean([ari(lab3, rng.integers(0,3,len(lab3))) for _ in range(200)]):+.5f}")

ARI(lab, itself)            = 1.000
ARI(lab, relabelled lab)    = 1.000   <- invariant to label names
ARI(lab, random labels)     = -0.0003  AMI = -0.0003  <- chance
ARI(lab, coarser 2-cluster) = 0.590
ARI over 200 random label vectors: mean +0.00004

The chance baseline is confirmed: random labels average zero over 200 draws and relabelling leaves the index at exactly 1. That is what makes ARI the right currency for comparing clusterings of the same objects, as Section 8 does for the compound library.

7.3 Stability under resampling

The deepest test an unsupervised method can take is: would a different sample of the same population have given the same partition?[19][20] Draw two random 80 % subsamples, cluster each independently, compare the labellings on the objects they share with ARI, and look at the distribution over repetitions.

# Stability: ARI between two independent 80% subsamples, 20 repetitions per K.
def stability_ari(X, K, reps=20, frac=0.8, seed=0):
    r = np.random.default_rng(seed); n = len(X); out = []
    for _ in range(reps):
        i1 = r.choice(n, int(frac*n), replace=False); i2 = r.choice(n, int(frac*n), replace=False)
        m1 = KMeans(K, n_init=5, random_state=0).fit(X[i1]); m2 = KMeans(K, n_init=5, random_state=0).fit(X[i2])
        both = np.intersect1d(i1, i2)
        out.append(ari(m1.predict(X[both]), m2.predict(X[both])))
    return np.array(out)
Xb, yb = make_blobs(n_samples=600, centers=4, cluster_std=0.6, random_state=0)   # genuine clusters
stab = {}
for K in [2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8]:
    stab[("descriptors", K)] = stability_ari(Zdesc, K)
for K in [3, 4, 5]:
    stab[("well-separated blobs", K)] = stability_ari(Xb, K)
for (name, K), v in stab.items():
    print(f"{name:22s} K={K}: stability ARI {v.mean():.3f} +- {v.std():.3f}  (min {v.min():.3f})")

# Figure 9: stability distributions, real descriptors vs genuinely clustered data.
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.2, 3.0))
pos, labels = [], []
for i, ((name, K), v) in enumerate(stab.items()):
    ax.boxplot(v, positions=[i], widths=.6,
               patch_artist=True,
               boxprops=dict(facecolor="#36c" if name == "descriptors" else "#2a8", alpha=.6))
    pos.append(i); labels.append(f"{'desc' if name=='descriptors' else 'blobs'}\nK={K}")
ax.set_xticks(pos); ax.set_xticklabels(labels, fontsize=7.5)
ax.set_ylabel("ARI between two 80% subsamples"); ax.set_ylim(0, 1.05)
ax.set_title("Stability is necessary but not sufficient"); ax.grid(alpha=.25, axis="y")
fig.tight_layout()

descriptors            K=3: stability ARI 0.915 +- 0.107  (min 0.480)
descriptors            K=4: stability ARI 0.759 +- 0.204  (min 0.357)
descriptors            K=5: stability ARI 0.916 +- 0.041  (min 0.822)
descriptors            K=6: stability ARI 0.753 +- 0.126  (min 0.525)
descriptors            K=8: stability ARI 0.826 +- 0.121  (min 0.603)
well-separated blobs   K=3: stability ARI 0.996 +- 0.008  (min 0.975)

Figure 9. ARI between two independent 80 % subsamples over 20 repetitions. Blue: ROCK1 descriptors; green: four well-separated synthetic blobs, where stability is essentially perfect at the correct K. The descriptor partitions are reproducible even though their silhouettes (Figure 8) say the clusters are not separated.

This is the subtlest result of the unit. A stable partition is not necessarily a real one. Cutting a smooth, elongated cloud at its waist reproduces beautifully across subsamples, because the cloud's shape is a stable property of the population; what is unstable is the number of pieces, not the boundary of any one. Stability therefore refutes a clustering but cannot confirm it.

8. The lab's first task: finding the chemical series

A chemist looking at 2,764 ROCK1 actives asks: how many distinct chemical ideas are here, and which compounds belong to each? Three answers follow, each from a different notion of similarity.

Butina/leader clustering[21] is the field's standard: count, for each molecule, how many neighbours lie within a cutoff $t$; sort by that count; then walk the list, and whenever a molecule is still unclaimed make it a cluster leader and claim all its unclaimed neighbours. One pass, no $K$, no pair closer than $t$ split apart, and a real molecule at every centre. In Morgan/ECFP4 space $t=0.35$ is the conventional "same series" cutoff. The alternatives compared here are average linkage on the same Tanimoto matrix and k-means on the raw bit vectors — chemically dubious, but what a general-purpose pipeline does by default.

The external reference is the Bemis-Murcko scaffold[23] already stored in the table: compounds sharing a scaffold share a core by construction.

# All pairwise Tanimoto distances, then Butina at several cutoffs.
t0 = time.perf_counter()
dists = []
for i in range(1, len(fps)):
    sims = DataStructs.BulkTanimotoSimilarity(fps[i], fps[:i])
    dists.extend([1 - s for s in sims])
dists = np.asarray(dists, dtype=np.float64)
print(f"{len(dists):,} Tanimoto distances in {time.perf_counter()-t0:.2f} s; "
      f"mean {dists.mean():.3f}, 1st percentile {np.percentile(dists,1):.3f}")
but = {}
rows = []
for cut in [0.2, 0.3, 0.35, 0.4, 0.5, 0.6]:
    cl = Butina.ClusterData(dists, len(fps), cut, isDistData=True)
    lab = np.zeros(len(fps), dtype=int)
    for ci, c in enumerate(cl):
        for i in c: lab[i] = ci
    but[cut] = lab
    rows.append({"cutoff": cut, "clusters": len(cl), "largest": len(cl[0]),
                 "singletons": sum(1 for c in cl if len(c) == 1),
                 "% in singletons": 100*sum(1 for c in cl if len(c) == 1)/len(fps)})
print(pd.DataFrame(rows).round(1).to_string(index=False))

Figure 10. Left: Butina cluster sizes on log-log axes for three cutoffs — heavy-tailed at every cutoff, a few large series and a long tail of singletons, the typical shape of a public bioactivity table. Right: adjusted Rand index between the four partitions; Butina agrees only moderately with the scaffold assignment, average linkage on the identical matrix hardly at all.

Three lessons sit in that matrix.

  1. Same distances, different algorithm, different answer. Average linkage and Butina use the identical matrix and the identical number of clusters, and their ARI is near zero: average linkage chains the sparse fingerprint space into one enormous cluster plus a crowd of singletons, while Butina's leader rule caps a cluster at the neighbourhood of one molecule.
  2. Clusters are not scaffolds. An ARI near 0.3 between Butina clusters and Bemis-Murcko scaffolds means they encode related but different notions of "same series" — the scaffold ignores every substituent, the fingerprint does not. When a referee asks for a "scaffold-based split", say which of the two you used.
  3. Granularity is a choice with consequences. Going from $t=0.2$ to $t=0.6$ changes the number of clusters about sixfold. No internal criterion picks $t$; the project does — the cutoff for buying one analogue per series is not the cutoff for a leave-cluster-out validation split[35].

      f"range {cmp_.loc[list(big),'pActivity'].min():.2f}-{cmp_.loc[list(big),'pActivity'].max():.2f} "
      f"(whole table: median {cmp_['pActivity'].median():.2f})")
sims_to_leader = [DataStructs.TanimotoSimilarity(fps[leader], fps[i]) for i in big]

9. The lab's second task: picking a diverse subset, and proving it

Suppose the budget allows 50 compounds for an orthogonal assay and the goal is coverage: no two picks should be near-duplicates. The right tool is not a clustering but a dissimilarity-based picker[24]; RDKit's MaxMinPicker starts from one molecule and repeatedly adds the molecule whose minimum distance to the already-picked set is largest. Claims of diversity are usually asserted; here we measure it against the only honest baseline, random selection of the same size, with a p-value by simulation.

# MaxMin diversity picking vs 200 random subsets of the same size.
NPICK = 50
picker = rdSimDivPickers.MaxMinPicker()
picked = list(picker.LazyBitVectorPick(fps, len(fps), NPICK, seed=0))
def set_distances(idx):
    '''All pairwise Tanimoto distances inside a subset.'''
    d = []
    for i in range(1, len(idx)):
        d.extend([1 - s for s in DataStructs.BulkTanimotoSimilarity(fps[idx[i]], [fps[j] for j in idx[:i]])])
    return np.asarray(d)
dp = set_distances(picked)
rand_sets = [list(rng.choice(len(fps), NPICK, replace=False)) for _ in range(200)]
dr = [set_distances(s) for s in rand_sets]
mean_r = np.array([d.mean() for d in dr]); min_r = np.array([d.min() for d in dr])
print(f"MaxMin pick : mean pairwise distance {dp.mean():.4f}, minimum pairwise distance {dp.min():.4f}")
print(f"random picks: mean {mean_r.mean():.4f} +- {mean_r.std():.4f} (200 sets), best random {mean_r.max():.4f}")
print(f"              their minimum pairwise distance averages {min_r.mean():.4f} "
      f"(i.e. a typical random set of 50 contains a near-duplicate pair)")
z = (dp.mean() - mean_r.mean())/mean_r.std()
print(f"z = {z:.1f} standard deviations above the random mean; "
      f"empirical p = {(mean_r >= dp.mean()).mean():.3f} (0 of 200 random sets reach it)")
print(f"distinct scaffolds: picked {cmp_.loc[picked,'scaffold_smiles'].nunique()} / {NPICK}, "
      f"random (mean) {np.mean([cmp_.loc[s,'scaffold_smiles'].nunique() for s in rand_sets]):.1f} / {NPICK}")

# Figure 12: the null distribution of diversity, and where the picked set falls.
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9.0, 3.0))
axes[0].hist(mean_r, bins=30, color="#999", alpha=.85, label="200 random sets of 50")
axes[0].axvline(dp.mean(), color="#c44", lw=2, label=f"MaxMin pick ({dp.mean():.3f})")
axes[0].set_xlabel("mean pairwise Tanimoto distance within the set")
axes[0].set_ylabel("sets"); axes[0].set_title("Diversity, measured against its null")
axes[0].legend(fontsize=7.5)
axes[1].hist(min_r, bins=30, color="#999", alpha=.85, label="random sets: closest pair")
axes[1].axvline(dp.min(), color="#c44", lw=2, label=f"MaxMin closest pair ({dp.min():.3f})")
axes[1].set_xlabel("minimum pairwise distance within the set")
axes[1].set_ylabel("sets"); axes[1].set_title("The redundancy a random pick buys")
axes[1].legend(fontsize=7.5)
fig.tight_layout()

              their minimum pairwise distance averages 0.2175 (i.e. a typical random set of 50 contains a near-duplicate pair)

Figure 12. Left: mean pairwise Tanimoto distance inside 200 random 50-compound subsets (grey) and inside the MaxMin pick (red); the pick lies outside the entire null distribution. Right: the same for the minimum pairwise distance — random subsets routinely contain near-identical pairs, the MaxMin set does not.

The mean distance moves only from about 0.84 to about 0.91, because in a 2,048-bit space almost every pair of unrelated molecules is already far apart. The second panel is where the money is: the closest pair in a random set of 50 is typically a near-twin, so assay wells are spent twice on one chemical idea. Report the minimum, not only the mean, when you claim a selection is diverse.

Exercise 3

Replace the MaxMin pick with "one compound per Butina cluster, largest clusters first" (a cluster-based pick) and compute the same two statistics. Which strategy gives the higher mean distance, and which guarantees that every large series is represented? Explain why a purchasing committee might prefer the second even though it scores worse on diversity.

10. The lab's third task: metastable conformations from a replica ensemble

Clustering the frames of a trajectory is how a structural project turns 500 pictures per run into "the protein visits three states, and here is a representative structure for each" — the input to a figure, a docking run or a Markov state model[26]. The classic comparison of algorithms for trajectories is Shao and co-workers'[25]; its practical conclusions (the metric matters more than the algorithm, and the result depends on how much of the trajectory you keep) are reproduced below. Our ensemble is deliberately awkward: six runs of only 1 ns. The coordinates are superposed on the minimised reference, so a Euclidean distance between flattened $20\times3$ vectors divided by $\sqrt{20}$ is the C-alpha RMSD in nanometres, and k-means can be applied directly.

# Frames as vectors; RMSD to the reference; PCA of the ensemble.
from sklearn.decomposition import PCA
Fmd = ca.reshape(len(ca), -1)                                  # (3000, 60)
ref = npz["ref_ca"]
rmsd_ref = np.sqrt(((ca - ref)**2).sum(-1).mean(-1))           # nm, = rmsd_ca_nm of the observables table
pca_md = PCA(n_components=10, random_state=0).fit(Fmd)
Ymd = pca_md.transform(Fmd)
print("mean C-alpha RMSD to the reference, per run (nm):")
print({r: round(float(rmsd_ref[run_of_frame == r].mean()), 3) for r in RUNS})
print(f"\nPCA of the 60-dimensional coordinate space: PC1 {pca_md.explained_variance_ratio_[0]:.1%}, "
      f"PC2 {pca_md.explained_variance_ratio_[1]:.1%}, "
      f"first two together {pca_md.explained_variance_ratio_[:2].sum():.1%}")

# Figure 13: the ensemble in PC space, coloured by run and by cluster, plus the cluster time series.
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(9.4, 3.0))
for i, r in enumerate(RUNS):
    m = run_of_frame == r
    axes[0].scatter(Ymd[m, 0], Ymd[m, 1], s=3, alpha=.6,
                    color=plt.cm.tab10(i), label=r)

    axes[2].plot(time_of_frame[m], lab_md[m] + 0.08*i, ".", ms=1.6, color=plt.cm.tab10(i))

Figure 13. Left: the 3,000 frames on the first two principal components of the C-alpha coordinates, coloured by run — the six runs occupy largely separate regions. Centre: the same projection coloured by the K = 4 clusters, which reproduce the run structure. Right: cluster index against time; most runs stay in one cluster for the whole nanosecond.

The table quantifies what the figure shows, and it is the key result: at $K=4$ the adjusted Rand index against run identity is about 0.5, against temperature below 0.1. The clusters are not metastable states of Trp-cage; they are the six trajectories. Each run relaxed from the same minimised structure into its own corner of shape space and stayed there (replica A3 near 0.25 nm RMSD, the others 0.10-0.19 nm), so a frame's cluster says which simulation it came from.

Domain context — why 1 ns is not enough, and what this costs

Trp-cage folds and unfolds on a timescale of microseconds; its experimental melting temperature is about 315 K. In 1 ns at 340 K the molecule has had time to jiggle, not to unfold. Worse, the frames within one run are strongly autocorrelated: the integrated autocorrelation time of the C-alpha RMSD in these runs is 36-171 ps, so a 1 ns run contains only about 3-14 statistically independent samples even though it contributes 500 rows to the table. Clustering treats every row as an independent object, which is why a per-frame clustering of a short ensemble recovers the replica structure: the between-replica differences are real and large, and the within-replica variation is small and correlated. Unit 20 develops the correct statistical treatment (block averaging, replica-level inference, convergence diagnostics). The honest sentence for a paper based on data like these is: "frames cluster by replica rather than by conformational state, indicating that 1 ns per replica does not sample the relevant transitions".

The machinery is still useful: the medoid frames printed above are genuine structures (not averages, which are geometrically distorted), annotated with their run and time, and each cluster's mean RMSD to its own centroid — all below about 0.09 nm — quantifies how tight the "state" is. That is the deliverable a structural project wants, provided the caption says "representative frame of cluster k" and not "conformational state k".

11. The lab's fourth task: are there patient subgroups?

The expression slice holds 138 biopsies: one diseased and one healthy gingival site from each of 69 patients[31]. The clinical question is whether the tissues fall into molecular subtypes — a claim made for this cohort[30]; the methodological question is what a clustering of 138 samples by 1,000 genes can support. Here we have an external label (clinical status), so every partition can be scored with ARI rather than admired. Genes are z-scored so that highly expressed genes do not dominate, and correlation distance (profile shape) is compared with Euclidean distance on z-scores.

# Patients and genes: build the matrix, then cluster it four ways.
NGENE = 1000
var_rank = expr.var(axis=1).sort_values(ascending=False)
sub_expr = expr.loc[var_rank.index[:NGENE]]                   # 1000 most variable genes x 138 samples
samples = list(sub_expr.columns)
status = (meta.loc[samples, "status"] == "diseased").astype(int).to_numpy()
Xg = sub_expr.T.to_numpy()                                    # samples x genes
Zg = StandardScaler().fit_transform(Xg)                       # z-score each gene
Dcorr = 1 - np.corrcoef(Xg)                                   # correlation distance between samples
print(f"{NGENE} genes x {len(samples)} samples; variance of the selected genes "
      f"{var_rank.iloc[:NGENE].min():.2f}-{var_rank.iloc[0]:.2f}")
print(f"correlation distance between samples: min {Dcorr[np.triu_indices(138,1)].min():.3f}, "
      f"median {np.median(Dcorr[np.triu_indices(138,1)]):.3f}, max {Dcorr[np.triu_indices(138,1)].max():.3f}")

results = {}
for meth in ["average", "complete", "ward"]:
    Lk = linkage(squareform(Dcorr, checks=False), method=meth)
    results[f"correlation + {meth}"] = fcluster(Lk, 2, criterion="maxclust") - 1
Lk_e = linkage(pdist(Zg), method="ward")
results["euclidean(z) + ward"] = fcluster(Lk_e, 2, criterion="maxclust") - 1
results["k-means on z-scores"] = KMeans(2, n_init=10, random_state=0).fit_predict(Zg)
Ypc = PCA(5, random_state=0).fit_transform(Zg)
results["k-means on 5 PCs"] = KMeans(2, n_init=10, random_state=0).fit_predict(Ypc)
for name, lab in results.items():
    print(f"{name:24s} sizes {np.bincount(lab)}  ARI vs diseased/healthy {ari(status, lab):.3f}")

axes[0].set_xlabel(f"PC1 ({pc.explained_variance_ratio_[0]:.0%})")
axes[0].set_ylabel(f"PC2 ({pc.explained_variance_ratio_[1]:.0%})")

    dn = dendrogram(Lk, no_labels=True, color_threshold=0, above_threshold_color="#444", ax=ax)
    cols = ["#c44" if status[i] == 1 else "#36c" for i in dn["leaves"]]
    ax.scatter(np.arange(len(cols))*10 + 5, np.full(len(cols), -0.01), c=cols, s=6, clip_on=False)
    ax.set_title(f"correlation + {meth}\nARI = {ari(status, fcluster(Lk,2,criterion='maxclust')):.2f}", fontsize=8.5)

Figure 14. Left: the 138 biopsies on their first two principal components; diseased (red) and healthy (blue) sites separate along PC1. Centre and right: dendrograms from the same correlation-distance matrix under average and Ward linkage, with each leaf's clinical status drawn underneath. Average linkage chains — its two-cluster cut isolates one outlying sample and leaves the other 137 together (ARI near zero) — while Ward splits the cohort into two comparable groups aligned with disease status.

Two methodological conclusions and one biological caution.

  • The linkage, not the distance, decided the answer. All three correlation-based clusterings used an identical matrix and only Ward recovered the clinical signal; a hierarchical clustering reported without its linkage is not reproducible.
  • An ARI of about 0.4 against a two-class label is moderate agreement, not a discovery. The dominant axis of variation in gingival tissue is inflammation, so unsupervised clustering rediscovers the label it was not given — a sanity check, not a subtype.
  • Subtype claims must respect the paired design. Each patient contributed two samples, so the 138 rows are not 138 independent observations; Unit 21 treats this with a paired model.

12. The clusters that are not there

The final hazard is visual. Non-linear embeddings — t-SNE and UMAP[27][28] — optimise a neighbourhood-preserving 2-D layout, and will produce visible groups whether or not the data contains any, because the optimisation pushes apart points that are not near neighbours. Distances between blobs, their sizes and even their number (which depends on perplexity) are not interpretable[27]; the single-cell genomics literature has been through a public reckoning on this point[29].

The experiment: take 400 points of pure 50-dimensional Gaussian noise — a data set with, by construction, exactly one cluster — embed it with t-SNE at three perplexities, run k-means on the embedding, and compute the silhouette of the resulting partition twice: in the embedding, and in the original data.

# Clusters that are not there: t-SNE of 400 points of pure noise.
from sklearn.manifold import TSNE
Xnoise = np.random.default_rng(1).normal(size=(400, 50))
noise_emb, noise_rows = {}, []
for perp in [5, 30, 100]:
    e = TSNE(n_components=2, random_state=0, init="pca", perplexity=perp).fit_transform(Xnoise)
    lab = KMeans(4, n_init=10, random_state=0).fit_predict(e)
    noise_emb[perp] = (e, lab)
    noise_rows.append({"perplexity": perp,
                       "silhouette in the embedding": silhouette_score(e, lab),
                       "silhouette of the same labels in the data": silhouette_score(Xnoise, lab)})
print(pd.DataFrame(noise_rows).round(3).to_string(index=False))
print("\nThe data is isotropic Gaussian noise: the true number of clusters is 1.")

# Figure 15: the same noise at three perplexities, with 4-means imposed on each embedding.
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(9.4, 3.0))
for ax, perp in zip(axes, [5, 30, 100]):
    e, lab = noise_emb[perp]
    ax.scatter(e[:, 0], e[:, 1], c=lab, s=7, cmap="viridis")
    ax.set_title(f"perplexity {perp}\nsilhouette {silhouette_score(e, lab):.2f} in map, "
                 f"{silhouette_score(Xnoise, lab):.2f} in data", fontsize=8.5)
    ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([])
fig.tight_layout()

Figure 15. t-SNE maps of 400 points of 50-dimensional Gaussian noise at three perplexities, coloured by k-means on the map itself. Every panel shows apparent islands with a silhouette in the map around 0.33-0.35 — the range a referee accepts as "well separated" — while the same labels score about 0.00-0.01 in the original data.

The rule that follows is simple and worth memorising.

Cluster in the data space; use the embedding only to display the clustering. Never cluster on t-SNE or UMAP coordinates, and never count blobs in a map.

The correct practice is below: t-SNE of the 2,764 compounds (after reducing the bits to 50 components), coloured by the Butina clusters computed from the full-dimensional Tanimoto distances.

# The right way round: cluster in fingerprint space, colour the embedding.

emb_fp = TSNE(n_components=2, random_state=0, init="pca", perplexity=30).fit_transform(Psvd)
print(f"t-SNE of {len(Xfp)} compounds in {time.perf_counter()-t0:.1f} s")
top_clusters = [c for c, _ in pd.Series(lab_butina).value_counts().head(6).items()]
print("six largest Butina clusters:", [(int(c), int((lab_butina == c).sum())) for c in top_clusters])
sil_fp_emb = silhouette_score(emb_fp, lab_butina)
print(f"silhouette of the Butina partition in the t-SNE map: {sil_fp_emb:.3f}; "
      f"in the Tanimoto space it was computed on: "
      f"{silhouette_score(Dsq, lab_butina, metric='precomputed'):.3f}")

Domain context — what "a cluster of actives" does and does not imply

A compact island of highly potent compounds is usually a publication artefact before it is a biological fact: one group published a series, optimised it to nanomolar potency and deposited forty analogues, so the cluster records the history of the field rather than a privileged region of chemical space. This is the bias that makes random splits optimistic in Unit 12, and why an applicability domain (Unit 17) is defined by distance to the training set.

13. Summary

Clustering cannot fail loudly: it always returns labels, and the labels always look like a finding, so the discipline has to come from the analyst. This unit built that discipline in five layers.

The metric is the model. Euclidean distance on standardised descriptors, Tanimoto on fingerprints[22], RMSD on superposed conformations and correlation on expression profiles answer four different questions about closeness, and distance matrices cost $O(n^2)$ memory.

Five algorithm families, each with its geometry. k-means assumes spherical, equal-spread, equal-size clusters and fails visibly on sheared, unequal-variance, unequal-size and non-convex data. Agglomerative clustering returns the whole family of partitions, and the linkage is a strong assumption: on an identical distance matrix, single/average and Ward can disagree almost completely (Sections 8 and 11). Density methods need no $K$ and allow noise, but a single $\varepsilon$ cannot serve several densities — HDBSCAN[12] was the only method to recover the two-density set. Gaussian mixtures add soft assignments and BIC[16]; a BIC that keeps falling means the density is not a mixture of a few separated Gaussians. Butina's leader algorithm[21] is the chemistry-specific tool: one pass, a real molecule at each centre, one interpretable cutoff.

Validity is three measurements, not one. Internal indices (silhouette[4], Davies-Bouldin[5]) presuppose convex clusters; external indices (ARI[17]) need a label and have a verified zero at chance; stability[20] refutes a partition but cannot confirm it, as the high stability of a low-silhouette partition showed. The elbow is not evidence — uniform noise produced the same bend, and only the gap statistic[7] reported "no structure" correctly.

The four lab tasks, honestly reported. Series detection gives a usable partition provided you state the fingerprint, metric, algorithm and cutoff and do not confuse clusters with scaffolds[23]. Diversity picking can be proved to work by simulation against random selection, and the minimum pairwise distance is the statistic that matters. Conformational clustering of a 1 ns replica ensemble recovers the replicas, a result about sampling rather than about the protein. Patient clustering recovers the clinical label it was not given, which is a sanity check rather than a subtype discovery.

The visual trap. t-SNE and UMAP will show islands in pure noise; the silhouette computed in the map was about ten times the silhouette of the same labels in the data[27][29]. Cluster in the data space, colour the map.

Everything here is computed from the public ROCK1 table[32] with scikit-learn[33], SciPy[34] and RDKit; what none of them provides is the decision about whether the answer means anything. Unit 16 takes up the same theme for supervised models — an explanation, like a clustering, is always produced, whether or not there is anything to explain.

14. Self-assessment

1. Why can inertia never be used to choose K, and what does the gap statistic add?

Inertia is the objective k-means minimises, and adding a centroid can only reduce it; the curve is monotone decreasing by construction, reaching zero when K = n. The gap statistic compares the observed log inertia with the log inertia of uniform reference data in the same bounding box, so it measures how much more structure the data has than a structureless null. In Section 7 the gap was flat at zero for uniform noise — correctly reporting "no clusters" where the elbow of the same data suggested K = 3.

2. A colleague clusters 2,000 compounds with k-means on raw 2,048-bit Morgan fingerprints and reports the centroid of each cluster as "the representative compound of the series". Give two distinct objections.

First, a centroid of binary vectors is a vector of fractions: it corresponds to no molecule and cannot be drawn, synthesised or docked, whereas a leader or medoid method returns a real compound. Second, squared Euclidean distance on sparse binary data is dominated by bits that are zero in both molecules — the shared absences Tanimoto deliberately ignores.

3. Single and average linkage are applied to the same Tanimoto distance matrix and give an ARI near zero. Is one of them wrong?

Neither is wrong; they encode different definitions of "close sets". Where almost all pairwise distances are large, both chain: each merge adds the nearest remaining point to a growing cluster, so any cut yields one giant cluster plus singletons — a correct execution of the rule and an unusable partition. Choose the linkage from the expected cluster shape before looking at results, and report it.

4. What does a mean silhouette of 0.29 tell you, and what does it hide?

It says that on average a point is only slightly closer to its own cluster than to the nearest other cluster — a weak partition. It hides the distribution: Figure 8 showed a substantial fraction of compounds with negative silhouettes (points that are closer to a neighbouring cluster than to their own) and at least one cluster whose mean is near zero. Always plot the per-point silhouettes.

5. Your clustering of 138 biopsies is highly stable under 80 % resampling. Can you conclude the subgroups are real?

No. Stability is necessary but not sufficient: a reproducible way of cutting a single elongated cloud in half is stable because the cloud's shape is a stable property of the population. Section 7.3 demonstrated exactly this on the descriptor data — high stability with low silhouette. Stability rules out partitions that are artefacts of one particular sample; it does not establish separation.

6. Why did clustering the MD frames recover the six runs instead of conformational states, and what would you change?

Each run relaxed from the same starting structure into its own region of shape space and stayed there, and consecutive frames are strongly autocorrelated (integrated autocorrelation times of 36-171 ps). The ARI against run identity was about 0.5, against temperature below 0.1. The fixes: microsecond trajectories, more replicas, a longer discarded equilibration, and clustering in a kinetically meaningful space (time-lagged independent components) rather than raw coordinates.

7. How would you choose the Butina cutoff for (a) buying one analogue per series and (b) building a leave-cluster-out validation split?

(a) A tight cutoff (small distance, e.g. 0.25-0.35) defines "the same chemical idea" narrowly, so one purchase per cluster still covers distinct ideas. (b) A looser cutoff (0.4-0.6) produces fewer, broader clusters, which makes the training and test sides of the split genuinely dissimilar and the estimate appropriately pessimistic; with a tight cutoff, near-neighbours of a test compound remain in training and the split is only nominally cluster-based.

8. Give the two statistics that should accompany any claim that a selected subset is diverse.

The mean pairwise distance within the subset and the minimum pairwise distance, each compared with the distribution obtained from many random subsets of the same size. Section 9 found the MaxMin pick about eight standard deviations above the random mean, with no random set of 200 reaching it; the minimum distance separated the two strategies far more sharply than the mean.

9. Why is Davies-Bouldin inappropriate for comparing a DBSCAN result with a k-means result?

Davies-Bouldin measures the ratio of within-cluster scatter to between-centroid distance, which assumes clusters are compact around a centroid. A crescent-shaped DBSCAN cluster has a large scatter about its centroid — which may not even lie inside the cluster — so the index penalises it regardless of how well it matches the data's geometry. Internal indices are only comparable between methods that share a notion of cluster shape; otherwise compare on an external label or on a downstream task.

10. A manuscript shows a UMAP of 5,000 compounds with eight visually distinct islands and concludes "eight chemotypes". What do you ask for?

A clustering performed in the original fingerprint space with a stated metric and algorithm; the silhouette of that partition computed in that space rather than in the embedding; the sensitivity of the picture to perplexity/n_neighbors and seed; and a negative control. Figure 15 showed four convincing islands in 50-dimensional Gaussian noise.

11. When is it correct to say "no clusters were found"?

When the evidence says so: no knee in the k-distance curve, no plateau in the eps sweep, a gap statistic indistinguishable from its null, low silhouettes at every K and no agreement with any external label — all five hold for the ROCK1 descriptor space. That sentence is publishable: it tells the next student not to repeat the analysis.

12. You must deliver "one representative conformation per state" to a colleague for docking. What do you hand over and why not the centroid?

The medoid: the real frame whose RMSD to the cluster centroid is smallest, with its run, time stamp, cluster population and the cluster's mean RMSD to its centroid. An average of coordinates distorts bond lengths and can collapse side chains, so it cannot be docked or deposited.

Glossary

Adjusted Rand index (ARI)
Agreement between two partitions corrected for chance: 0 for random agreement, 1 for identity.
Butina (leader) clustering
Single-pass clustering in which molecules sorted by neighbour count become cluster leaders and claim all unclaimed neighbours within a distance cutoff.
Centroid / medoid
The mean of a cluster's members (may not be a real object) / the member closest to that mean (always a real object).
Cophenetic correlation
Correlation between original distances and the dendrogram heights at which pairs merge.
Davies-Bouldin index
Mean over clusters of the worst ratio of within-cluster scatter to between-centroid distance; lower is better.
DBSCAN
Density-based clustering with a radius and a minimum-point count; produces arbitrary shapes and explicit noise labels.
Elbow heuristic
Choosing K where the inertia curve stops falling steeply; it has no null model and bends even for structureless data.
Gap statistic
Difference between the expected log inertia of uniform reference data and the observed log inertia; zero means no more structure than noise.
Gaussian mixture model
Generative model of the data as a weighted sum of multivariate normals, fitted by expectation-maximisation, giving soft cluster memberships.
HDBSCAN
Hierarchical extension of DBSCAN that extracts the clusters most persistent across density levels, allowing clusters of different density.
Inertia
Within-cluster sum of squared distances to centroids; the k-means objective, monotone decreasing in K.
Linkage
Rule defining the distance between two clusters in agglomerative clustering (single, complete, average, Ward).
Metastable conformation
A region of conformational space a molecule lingers in, relative to the time needed to cross between regions.
Responsibility
In a mixture model, the posterior probability that a given component generated a given observation.
RMSD
Root-mean-square deviation between two superposed structures; a Euclidean distance normalised by the number of atoms.
Silhouette
Per-object index comparing its mean distance to its own cluster with that to the nearest other cluster; ranges from -1 to 1.
Stability (of a clustering)
Agreement, measured by ARI, between partitions obtained from independent resamples of the same data.
Tanimoto (Jaccard) coefficient
Shared bits divided by the union of set bits of two binary fingerprints; ignores bits absent from both.
t-SNE / UMAP
Non-linear embeddings that preserve local neighbourhoods for visualisation; distances and apparent clusters in the map are not quantitatively interpretable.
Ward linkage
Agglomerative rule that merges the pair of clusters causing the smallest increase in within-cluster sum of squares; defined for Euclidean distances only.
